evidence_text: The abstract places the paper squarely in the topic area, since it describes the MediaEval 2020 task of predicting short-term and long-term video memorability, along with the dataset, evaluation metrics, and task requirements. However, it says nothing about audio gestalt features or about combining audio with visual and semantic cues, so it does not directly ground the claim that audio integration improves short-term memorability prediction over visual and semantic features alone.

The abstract is topically related, since it addresses the MediaEval 2020 Predicting Media Memorability task and names high-dynamic video content and limited dataset size as core challenges. It does not mention audio features, gestalt features, or any multimodal combination of audio with visual and semantic cues, and it reports no results comparing such combinations against visual and semantic features alone, so it does not directly ground the research question.

The abstract describes a multimodal late-fusion approach that combines visual, semantic, and auditory features and uses audio gestalt to estimate the audio modality's influence on video memorability, which directly addresses the question's premise of integrating audio gestalt with visual and semantic cues for memorability prediction. It does not report results or a comparison against visual and semantic features alone, so it grounds the premise but not evidence of improvement.

The abstract is topically related, since it covers predicting short-term and long-term video memorability and notes that the 2020 videos are action-rich content from the TRECVid 2019 Video-to-Text dataset. It says nothing about audio narration, emotional cues, or educational videos, so it offers no grounding for how emotional cues in narration affect memorability. The mention of action-rich videos only loosely touches the "non-narrated, action-rich" comparison group in the question.

This directly supports the question's premise that quality attention can drive user-adaptive, unpaired enhancement. The summary does not mention perceptual priors or the combined framework, so it grounds only the quality-attention part of the premise.

This directly supports the question's premise that unpaired enhancement can balance content fidelity with quality improvement. It does not mention perceptual priors, QAGAN's quality attention, or user adaptivity, so it grounds only part of the premise.
